extracted.intended_audience: graduate students, scholars, and researchers in communication and cultural studies
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluative criteria for theorizing and doing research in communication and popular culture, contrasting transmission/ritual views and three methodological strategies (behavioral, formal, cultural). Useful for assessing the scope, method, and explanatory adequacy of communication research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid labeling the field 'mass communications' (Williams's critique)
rubrics_metrics.description: The term 'mass communications' is damaging because it (1) limits study to specialized areas (broadcasting, film, 'popular literature') while ignoring the whole common area of discourse in speech and writing; (2) privileges the weak notion of 'mass' audience and obscures specific communication situations and conventions; (3) encourages research that asks only whether media influence or corrupt people, favoring impact/effects studies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer broader labels (e.g., 'culture' or 'contemporary culture') and broaden empirical focus beyond media effects to include practices, conventions, and forms of everyday discourse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigate communication as practices, conventions, and forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Communication should be studied first as a set of practices, conventions, and forms rather than assumed background conditions; these forms (speech, writing, ritual, art) require direct investigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Research should analyze the forms and conventions themselves (their shapes, vocabularies, genres, usages) instead of only measuring downstream 'effects' on audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transmission (transportation) view of communication
rubrics_metrics.description: Communication conceived as transmitting messages across distance for purposes of control: persuasion, attitude change, behavior modification, socialization via information/influence/conditioning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This view centers on empirical questions about how media influence audiences and on measurable psychological and sociological conditions for attitude/behavior change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ritual view of communication
rubrics_metrics.description: Communication conceived as the process through which a shared culture is created, maintained, and transformed; focused on ritual, mythology, art, and literature as practices that maintain society in time and create shared beliefs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt interpretive approaches that examine how symbolic forms produce collective meaning and fellowship rather than only their spatial transmission effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyze the relation between expressive forms and social order
rubrics_metrics.description: Scholars should treat cultural forms (religion, ideology, journalism, art) as objects that make sense of life and relate those meanings systematically to social order and historical patterns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to 'figure out what it means' in the way a literary critic does with a novel—identify claims, meanings, and interrelations among cultural forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Face Mannheim's Paradox (distrust of reason) explicitly
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize the dilemma of where ideology leaves off and science begins: whether scientific accounts are themselves shaped by interests, conditioning, or unconscious forces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methodological choices should be justified as strategies for handling this paradox rather than assumed neutral; reflect on how methods attempt to escape or confront the paradox.

rubrics_metrics.name: Behavioral science strategy (causal/laws approach)
rubrics_metrics.description: Conceive communication as a behavioral science aimed at elucidating laws: causal explanations (interest theory) derive ideology from social structure; functional/strain explanations derive ideology from needs or functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of limits: causal models often yield low predictive correlations and functional models risk obscurity or ad hoc functional attributions; common escapes from Mannheim include claiming statistical generality or claiming the scientist is exempt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal science strategy (structure/competence approach)
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop formal theories that explain deep structures (e.g., linguistic competence, systems of symbolic opposition) rather than predicting behavior or performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use formal models (linguistics, systems theory, structuralism) to build theoretical mechanisms that can account for symbolic regularities; this avoids some problems of causal behavioral explanations but may be abstract and difficult to operationalize.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural science strategy (interpretive/meaning approach)
rubrics_metrics.description: Approach communication as a cultural science whose objective is to elucidate meaning—treat symbolic systems as ordered, heterogeneous systems of symbols to be interpreted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ interpretive, critical, and comparative methodologies (anthropological/literary) to render cultural phenomena intelligible in their own terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideology: causal/interest explanations
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain ideology by rooting it in social structure and group interests—predict ideological positions from class membership or other antecedent variables.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that such causal accounts may be intuitively appealing but empirically weak (low correlations) and risk essentialism ('one class, one ideology').

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideology: strain/functional explanations
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain ideology as a response to chronic malintegration—ideology functions to relieve tensions or restore equilibrium (catharsis, displacement onto symbolic enemies).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use functional accounts to show how ideology serves psychic or social needs, but beware of post hoc functional attributions that explain everything without predictive specificity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not dispose of symbolic phenomena by naming them 'laws' or 'functions' prematurely
rubrics_metrics.description: Behavioral and functional strategies often 'dispose of the phenomenon in the very act of naming it' by flattening rich symbolic life into scientific prose that assumes disinterest/objectivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preserve the complexity of symbolic forms—avoid reducing art, ideology, religion, and popular culture to simple causal or utilitarian explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demand empirical adequacy and beware weak predictive power
rubrics_metrics.description: Antecedent-causal models of mass communication typically show modest correlations (often < 0.5) and inability to predict individual outcomes reliably; research must acknowledge these empirical limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret statistical associations cautiously; do not overclaim causal determinism from weak correlations; consider complementary methods that capture meaning and context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broaden scope to include everyday expressive and ritual forms beyond mass media
rubrics_metrics.description: Studies should include literature, art, religion, conversation, sport and other expressive forms—not only products explicitly transmitted by mass media.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design research agendas that integrate media with non-media cultural practices to understand culture as a whole way of life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt methodologies from anthropology and literary criticism for interpretive depth
rubrics_metrics.description: Methodologically, the study of culture benefits from critical, interpretive, and comparative methods central to anthropology and literary studies rather than only quantitative impact studies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use close interpretive work, comparative analysis, and ethnographic sensitivity (e.g., Geertzian thick description) when studying symbolic systems and meanings.
